p1s1.text: Imagine trying to read a story while chairs move across the floor and students talk around you.

p1s2.text: You may read the same sentence several times without understanding it.

p1s3.text: Noise can make it difficult to concentrate, which means keeping your attention on what you are doing.

p1s4.text: This problem can affect students in both public and private schools.

p2s1.text: Noise may come from inside or outside the classroom.

p2s2.text: Talking, moving furniture and loud fans can disturb a lesson.

p2s3.text: Traffic and building work nearby can also make it hard to hear the teacher.

p2s4.text: When students miss important instructions, they may make mistakes even when they understand the subject.

p3s1.text: Some people think that private schools are always quieter than public schools.

p3s2.text: However, the type of school is not enough to tell us how noisy it is.

p3s3.text: A small private school next to a busy road may be noisier than a large public school on a quiet street.

p3s4.text: The number of students in a room and their behavior also make a difference.

p4s1.text: Noise does not affect every student in the same way.

p4s2.text: Some can work with quiet sounds around them, while others need more silence.

p4s4.text: During a test, students usually need quiet.

p4s5.text: During group work, however, talking helps students share ideas.

p4s6.text: A completely silent classroom is therefore not always the best place to learn.

p5s1.text: Schools can take simple steps to reduce noise.

p5s2.text: They can put soft covers under chair legs and close windows during noisy activities outside.

p5s3.text: Teachers can also agree on clear rules with their classes, such as speaking one at a time.

p5s4.text: Both public and private schools should provide quiet spaces for students who need them.
